rules.title: Timeout and retry cap on every remote call
rules.what: Every call to another service has an explicit timeout and a bounded retry policy (max attempts, backoff, jitter); no call without a deadline.
rules.why: An unbounded call holds its connection, thread and memory for as long as the failure lasts, and unbounded retries multiply the very load that caused the failure.
rules.how: Set a per-call timeout from the SLO; retry only idempotent operations, cap attempts, back off with jitter; circuit-break repeated failures.

patterns.note: requests call without visible timeout kwarg in the call or session; verify a default timeout exists.
Retry loop with fixed sleep; check backoff+jitter and max attempts.

verify.how: Mock service that hangs: the caller aborts within the timeout; a failing service gets at most N retries.

limits: Timeouts longer than the user-facing SLA are wasted work even when they eventually succeed.

rules.title: Bound every loop, queue and pool
rules.what: Every loop, queue, cache and pool that can grow has an explicit bound; work that can be rejected is rejected cleanly.
rules.why: Unbounded collections are the standard way backends die: the queue grows until memory goes, the retry storm until the service melts. Bounds convert a crash into a controlled failure.
rules.how: Set max sizes on queues/pools/caches, max iterations on data-driven loops, and backpressure (reject, shed, or persist) at the boundaries.

patterns.note: Infinite loop; verify a break/exit condition exists.
Unbounded queue constructed; check maxsize declaration.

verify.how: Overload test: pushing beyond the bound fails cleanly (rejection or backpressure), not with OOM.

rules.title: Cache stable results with explicit invalidation
rules.what: Cache or precompute results that are requested repeatedly and stable between requests; state the invalidation trigger and the maximum size at creation.
rules.why: Recomputing the same answer burns the same CPU on every request. The cost of the cache (memory, staleness) must be stated, but for stable data it is almost always lower than recomputation.
rules.how: Identify hot paths with measurements, cache their results, document key, TTL, size and what invalidates them (NR-ARCH-006).

verify.how: Hit rate measured on the target path; recompute count per unit of work decreased.

limits: Personalised or volatile data may cache worse than it computes; measure the hit rate before claiming the win.

rules.title: Paginate and stream, never return unbounded results
rules.what: Any endpoint or query that can return a large collection paginates (default and max page size) or streams; no unbounded array answers.
rules.why: An unbounded response couples the service's memory to the size of its largest dataset; it fails on the day the data grows, after working for years.
rules.how: Default page size (e.g. 20-50) and a hard max (e.g. 100); cursor-based pagination for stable ordering; streaming for exports.

patterns.note: ORM .all() without slicing; verify a limit or pagination upstream.

verify.how: Test with more items than the max page: response is bounded and a next-cursor is provided.

limits: Admin exports may need full dumps; they stream and are exempted deliberately.

rules.title: Sober logging, bounded retention
rules.what: Log what is needed to operate and debug, at the right level; no sensitive or excessive payloads; retention set per log class.
rules.why: Logging everything is storage and transfer forever, plus a legal risk. Logging nothing is un-operable. The right level is a deliberate choice per event type.
rules.how: Structured logs with a level policy; sample high-frequency events; never log secrets or raw personal data; set retention per class (NR-CONTENT-007).

patterns.note: Potential sensitive data in a log call; REVIEW.

verify.how: Log schema reviewed: levels policy, no sensitive fields, retention configured.

rules.title: Release resources on every path
rules.what: Files, connections, locks and transactions are released on the error path too: context managers, finally blocks, defer; fail fast and clean.
rules.why: A resource held through a failure path stays held: connection pools drain, file handles run out, locks stall other workers. The error path is the common path under load.
rules.how: Use context managers (with, defer, using, try-with-resources) systematically; fail fast rather than zombie-waiting; verify pool metrics under fault injection.

patterns.note: open() without a with-statement on the same line; verify closure.

verify.how: Fault-injection run: pool/handle usage returns to baseline after failures.

rules.title: Prefer events over polling
rules.what: Do not poll a state that can be pushed: use webhooks, events, change data capture, or long-poll done properly instead of fixed-interval re-checking.
rules.why: Polling spends requests proportional to time rather than to change; most of them return nothing new, on both sides of the connection.
rules.how: Map polling loops in the codebase and the integration surface; replace with push where the source supports it; keep polling only for sources without push, at a justified interval.

patterns.note: Polling interval; check whether the source offers a push mechanism.
Sleep-based polling loop; candidate for event-driven redesign.

verify.how: Requests per state change measured before/after; polling eliminated or interval justified in writing.

limits: Some systems (SMTP checks, file drops) have no push; documented polling is the honest fallback.

rules.title: Compute derived data once
rules.what: Do not store or recompute the same derived data in two places; compute it once, at the point where the cost is lowest, and reference it.
rules.why: Duplicated derived data doubles write cost and drifts out of sync; duplicated recomputation doubles read cost forever. Both are taxes paid on every request.
rules.how: Identify data computed from the same inputs in several code paths; extract to one function, service or precomputed store; document the refresh policy.

verify.how: Derived-data inventory: each computed value has one producing site.

limits: Denormalisation for measured read performance is legitimate; it is documented as a decision with its refresh path.

rules.title: Connection pools sized and shared
rules.what: Database and service clients use a shared pool sized to the real concurrency; no per-request connections, no unbounded pool growth.
rules.why: Per-request connections exhaust the database's own limits under modest load; unbounded pools move the failure to the database instead of protecting it.
rules.how: One pool per process, max size from the database's capacity and the app's concurrency, with acquire timeouts and metrics.

patterns.note: Direct connection creation inside request scope; candidate for pooling.

verify.how: Pool metrics under load: acquire wait bounded, database connection count stable.

limits: Serverless/short-lived runtimes may need HTTP-based drivers or external poolers; state the constraint.

rules.title: Incremental, restartable pipelines
rules.what: Batch and pipeline work is incremental (only what changed) and restartable from a checkpoint, not all-or-nothing.
rules.why: A full-recompute pipeline pays its whole cost at every run and again at every failure; an incremental one pays for the delta only.
rules.how: Track processed state, cut work into resumable units, checkpoint progress, recompute only what changed upstream.

verify.how: Run cost proportional to the change size; interruption resumes without redoing completed units.

limits: Checkpointing adds state complexity; proportion it to the pipeline's real duration and cost.
